items.key_text:
Explain the seven layers of the OSI reference model and state the main function of
each layer. (10 marks)
Model Answer:
The OSI model has 7 layers (top to bottom):
• Application (7): Provides network services to user applications (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS).
• Presentation (6): Data translation, encryption/decryption and compression.
• Session (5): Establishes, manages and terminates sessions; handles synchronisation.
• Transport (4): End-to-end delivery, segmentation, flow control, error control, port addressing
(TCP/UDP).
• Network (3): Logical (IP) addressing, routing and path selection; unit is the packet.
• Data Link (2): Framing, physical (MAC) addressing, error detection and media access control; unit
is the frame.
• Physical (1): Transmission of raw bits over the medium; voltage levels, cables, connectors, bit
synchronisation.
Marking: 1 mark for correct order of all layers; 1 mark per layer function (7); 2 marks for PDU/clarity and
presentation.
items.student_answer:
Explain the seven layers of the OSI reference model and state the main function of
each layer. (10 marks)
Answer:
The OSI model has seven layers. They are Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session,
Presentation and Application.
Physical layer sends the bits over the cable. Data Link layer does framing and also error detection
using MAC address. Network layer is used for routing the packets using IP address and it also does
error detection and correction of data. Transport layer provides end to end delivery of data and
breaks the data into segments. Session layer sets up and closes the session between two
computers. Presentation layer is used for encryption and also for converting the data to the format of
the application. Application layer is where the user works, for example browser and email.

items.summary: The student's answer is largely correct in terms of covering the layers of the OSI model but lacks the specific functions for each layer and is not as clear as the model answer.

items.key_text:
Differentiate between TCP and UDP with any four points and give one application
of each. (10 marks)
Model Answer:
Differences between TCP and UDP:
• Connection: TCP is connection-oriented (3-way handshake); UDP is connectionless.
• Reliability: TCP is reliable (acknowledgements, retransmission, ordered delivery); UDP is
unreliable with no guarantee of delivery or order.
• Speed/Overhead: TCP has a 20-byte header and higher overhead, so it is slower; UDP has an
8-byte header and is faster.
• Flow and congestion control: TCP provides both; UDP provides none.
• Applications: TCP - HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, email. UDP - DNS, VoIP, video streaming, online
gaming.
Marking: 2 marks per correct difference (4 points = 8 marks); 1 mark each for the TCP and UDP application
examples.
items.student_answer:

of each. (10 marks)
Answer:
TCP is connection oriented and UDP is connectionless. TCP uses a three way handshake before
sending data. TCP is reliable because it sends acknowledgements and resends lost data.
UDP is more reliable than TCP because it does not have much overhead, and TCP is faster than
UDP because it checks everything. UDP header is 8 bytes and TCP header is 20 bytes.
Example of TCP is HTTP and web browsing. Example of UDP is DNS and video streaming.

items.key_text:
A network has the address 192.168.10.0/24. Divide it into 4 equal subnets. Find the
subnet mask, block size, usable hosts per subnet, and the network, first host, last
host and broadcast address of each subnet. (10 marks)
Model Answer:
Given: 192.168.10.0/24, 4 equal subnets requires borrowing 2 bits (22 = 4).
• New prefix = /26, subnet mask = 255.255.255.192.
• Block size = 256 - 192 = 64.
• Usable hosts per subnet = 26 - 2 = 62.
• Subnet 1: Network 192.168.10.0, hosts .1 - .62, broadcast 192.168.10.63
• Subnet 2: Network 192.168.10.64, hosts .65 - .126, broadcast 192.168.10.127
• Subnet 3: Network 192.168.10.128, hosts .129 - .190, broadcast 192.168.10.191
• Subnet 4: Network 192.168.10.192, hosts .193 - .254, broadcast 192.168.10.255
Marking: Mask 2 marks; block size 1 mark; usable hosts 2 marks; four subnet ranges 1.25 marks each (5
marks total, rounded).

items.key_text:
Explain the working of CSMA/CD used in Ethernet, including the role of the jam
signal and binary exponential backoff. (10 marks)
Model Answer:
CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) is the MAC method of classic
half-duplex Ethernet (IEEE 802.3).
• Carrier sense: A station listens to the medium; if idle it transmits, if busy it waits.
• Multiple access: Many stations share the same medium, so two may transmit at the same time.
• Collision detection: While transmitting, the station monitors the line; a signal different from what
it sent indicates a collision.
• Jam signal: On detecting a collision the station sends a short jam signal (32 bits) so all stations
know a collision occurred.
• Binary exponential backoff: After the n-th collision a station waits a random number of slot times
chosen from 0 to 2n - 1 (n capped at 10), and gives up after 16 attempts.
• Not used in Wi-Fi, which uses CSMA/CA because collisions cannot be detected reliably on a
wireless medium.
Marking: Carrier sense/multiple access 2; collision detection 2; jam signal 2; backoff 3; clarity 1.
items.student_answer:
Explain the working of CSMA/CD used in Ethernet, including the role of the jam
signal and binary exponential backoff. (10 marks)
Answer:
CSMA/CD means Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection. It is used in Ethernet and
also in Wi-Fi networks.
First the station senses the channel. If the channel is free it sends the data, otherwise it waits. If two
stations send at same time a collision happens. When collision is detected the station stops and
sends a jam signal so that other stations also know about the collision. After that the station waits for
some random time and tries again.

justifications.Semantic accuracy: The student's explanation is mostly accurate but contains some minor errors such as stating CSMA/CD is used in Wi-Fi networks, which is incorrect. The explanation of binary exponential backoff is also not clear.
justifications.Completeness: The student's answer is incomplete as it does not cover the role of the jam signal and binary exponential backoff, which are crucial parts of the CSMA/CD protocol.
justifications.Clarity: The student's answer is unclear and lacks structure. The explanation of CSMA/CD is somewhat disjointed and does not flow well.

items.key_text:
Compare Distance Vector routing and Link State routing. Name one protocol and
the algorithm used by each. (10 marks)
Model Answer:
Distance Vector: Each router knows only its neighbours and its own distance table; it periodically
sends its whole routing table to directly connected neighbours only. Based on the Bellman-Ford
algorithm. Example protocol: RIP. Slow convergence, count-to-infinity problem, suitable for small
networks.
Link State: Each router discovers its neighbours, builds link-state advertisements (LSAs) and floods
them to all routers in the area, so every router has the complete topology map. Each router then
runs Dijkstra's shortest path first algorithm. Example protocol: OSPF. Faster convergence, more
memory/CPU, suitable for large networks.
Marking: DV description 3; LS description 3; algorithms 2; protocols 1; comparison points
(convergence/scalability) 1.
items.student_answer:
Compare Distance Vector routing and Link State routing. Name one protocol and
the algorithm used by each. (10 marks)
Answer:
In Distance Vector routing each router sends its routing table to all the routers in the network. It uses
Dijkstra algorithm. Example of Distance Vector protocol is RIP. It is used for small networks.
In Link State routing each router knows only its neighbours and the routing table is shared with
neighbours only. It uses Bellman Ford algorithm. Example is OSPF. Link state converges faster than
distance vector.

justifications.Concept coverage: The student correctly identified the two routing types and their main characteristics, but missed some details such as the Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra algorithms, and the suitability for different network sizes.
justifications.Semantic accuracy: The student's description of the algorithms and protocols is mostly accurate, but there are some minor errors like using 'routing table' instead of 'distance table' for Distance Vector and 'neighbours' instead of 'neighboring routers' for Link State.
justifications.Completeness: The student did not provide a comparison of the two routing types, nor did they mention the count-to-infinity problem for Distance Vector or the scalability issues for Link State.
justifications.Clarity: The student's answer is somewhat unclear due to the use of 'routing table' instead of 'distance table' and the lack of a clear distinction between the two routing types.

items.summary: The student provided a basic understanding of Distance Vector and Link State routing, but failed to cover all the required points and maintain a high level of accuracy and clarity.
